```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5,
                      warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

A DietView sunburst shows the diet at seven ranks at once, from kingdom at the
center to species at the edge. This article explains what a percentage in any
ring is a percentage of, and why prey that could not be identified to a given
rank stay in the figure instead of being dropped. It uses the invented example
table that ships with the package (24 prey records from 11 stomachs), so the
numbers illustrate the bookkeeping, not the diet of these fish.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)

dat <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
lin <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example_lineage.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
spec <- dv_spec(predator = "predator_species_common_name", stomach = "stomach_id",
                prey_id = "aphia_id", prey_name = "verified_name",
                weight = "prey_weight", digestion = "digestion_level_id")
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lin, verbose = FALSE)
tree <- dv_build_tree(prep$data, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
```

## One record, one place in every ring

`dv_build_tree()` gives every record one place at every rank: the taxon
it was identified to at that rank or, if identification stopped earlier, an
unidentified node (`NA` in the tables) below the last rank it reached. A
shrimp named *Pandalus borealis* sits under Decapoda at order and under
*Pandalus* at genus. A record named only "Decapoda" sits under Decapoda at
order and in the unidentified node below Decapoda at family, genus and species.

So every ring holds the same records and the same weight:

```{r totals}
rings <- unique(tree$rank)
data.frame(
  rank      = rings,
  records   = sapply(rings, function(r) sum(tree$value_occ[tree$rank == r])),
  weight_g  = sapply(rings, function(r) round(sum(tree$value_w[tree$rank == r]), 1)),
  pct_total = sapply(rings, function(r) round(sum(tree$pct_occ[tree$rank == r]), 1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

Each percentage in the tree (`pct_occ` for records, `pct_w` for weight) is a
node's value divided by that common total, and each ring adds up to 100%.
Because no record is lost between rings, a node's value is also the sum of its
children's values, which is what lets the rings nest:

```{r nesting}
kids <- tapply(tree$value_occ, tree$parent, sum)
parents <- tree[tree$id %in% names(kids), ]
all.equal(parents$value_occ, as.numeric(kids[parents$id]))
```

## What dropping the unidentified records would do

The usual alternative is to drop, at each rank, the records that were not
identified to that rank, and to compute shares among the rest. Each ring then
has its own total, and the rings stop agreeing with each other:

```{r dropped}
id_only <- function(r) tree[tree$rank == r & tree$label != "NA", ]
cl <- id_only("Class"); od <- id_only("Order")
mal_class <- 100 * sum(cl$value_occ[cl$label == "Malacostraca"]) / sum(cl$value_occ)
mal_order <- 100 * sum(od$value_occ[grepl("|Malacostraca|", od$id, fixed = TRUE)]) /
             sum(od$value_occ)
round(c(class_ring = mal_class, order_ring = mal_order), 1)
```

Malacostraca would be `r round(mal_class, 1)`% of the identified records at
class, while its three orders together would be `r round(mal_order, 1)`% of the
identified records at order. Nothing about the diet changed between the two
rings; only the set of records did. With the unidentified records kept,
Malacostraca and its orders hold the same 11 records in both rings.

## How much was not identified

`dv_rank_table()` lists one ring. At order, there is one unidentified row per
parent: under Bivalvia, Polychaeta, Copepoda and the fish class, plus the
material that could not be placed at all.

```{r na}
ord <- dv_rank_table(tree, "Order")
ord[ord$label == "NA", ]
sum(ord$pct_occ[ord$label == "NA"])
```

Here `r round(sum(ord$pct_occ[ord$label == "NA"]), 1)`% of the records are
unidentified at order. Report that figure next to any statement made at that
rank: an order-level description of this diet rests on the remaining
`r round(100 - sum(ord$pct_occ[ord$label == "NA"]), 1)`%.

## The figures

Records first, then weight. The two currencies often rank prey differently,
so look at both before choosing one to report.

```{r sunburst-occ}
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "occurrence", title = "All predators",
            subtitle = "share of prey records")
```

```{r sunburst-w}
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "weight", title = "All predators",
            subtitle = "share of prey weight")
```

White wedges with gray edges are records not identified at that rank. Hovering over a wedge
shows its count and its share of the ring.

## Colors

`dv_palette()` gives each taxon name one color and unidentified nodes white.
Build it once from all the records and pass it to every figure you want to
compare, so the same taxon has the same color everywhere:

```{r palette}
pal <- dv_palette(tree$label)
head(pal)
```

The palette has 20 colors and reuses them when there are more taxa, so in a
large survey two taxa can share a color. Check the hover labels before you
read a color as a taxon.

`dv_palette_tree()` is the alternative for large surveys. It gives one hue to
each phylum (the second rank) and lighter tints of that hue to its
descendants, and keeps unidentified nodes white. Its colors are keyed by node,
so build it from the pooled tree and pass it to every panel in the same way:

```{r palette-tree}
pal_tree <- dv_palette_tree(tree)
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "occurrence", colors = pal_tree, title = "All predators",
            subtitle = "share of prey records, colors by phylum")
```
